messages.subject: New release: simmer 3.8.0
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A new release hit CRAN yesterday, and Windows binaries are already
available for r-devel and r-release. This release includes two new
major features that have been discussed in this list.

The first of them is a new data source that allows us to attach a data
frame to a trajectory. For each row, the simulator creates a new
arrival: one column must contain the (relative or absolute) arrival
time, and the other columns can be used to automatically initialise
priorities and attributes. And of course, this data source can be
combined with dynamic generators. See ?add_dataframe for further
details.

The second feature is the ability to offload monitoring data to disk
(to CSV files). By default, monitoring is still performed in memory,
but now we can change that in the simulator instantiation. See ?simmer
and ?monitor for further information and examples on how to define and
use an on-disk monitor.

Please, take a look at the changelog for a comprehensive list of changes:

https://r-simmer.org/news/index.html#simmer-3-8-0

Regards,
Iñaki

Hello,

I am working through a trajectory that has arrivals flow sequentially through a path of resources each with individual capacity and queue limits. I want to ensure that an arrival does not release a resource until it can get a spot in queue or server at the next one. I am using a rollback as detailed in some vignettes to keep the arrival from being rejected when the queue is full . Then the next step in the trajectory after the seize is the release of the 1st resource. I noticed that the log of the arrivals by resource records the 1st resource to be finished only once the arrival gets out of the queue at the second resource. This implies that the arrival is taking up capacity both in the queue at the second resource as well as in the server at the 1st. I would like the arrival to release capacity at the 1st as soon as it can get a spot in the queue at the next resource.

Will a seize only be successful if there is capacity available in the server and not just the queue?
Is there some argument or functionality I can use to get around that?

Thanks in advance for your help!

> Created a simulation that runs for short run times and "Error in
> run_(private$sim_obj) ..." for longer run times.

Note that you will always see that whenever a simulation fails for
whatever reason, simply because the "run" method is *the* method you
call to start the simulation. So for R, it's *the* method that raises
the error, although it's happening in another place: in a trajectory.
But the important bit is the message afterwards (see below).

> What is the definition of this error and is there a reason it occurs for
> longer run times.
>
> Why is it occurring for longer run times:
>
> simulation %>% run(5000)
> simmer environment: anonymous | now: 5000 | next: 5052.27699025771
>
>
> simulation %>% run(7000)
> Error in run_(private$sim_obj, until) : Expecting a single value:
> [extent=0].

This is the error: "Expecting a single value: [extent=0]".
Unfortunately, the runtime is pretty complex (R calling C++ calling R
again), so it's almost impossible to display a meaningful error
telling you where exactly the error is (at the high level).
Fortunately, the message issued by Rcpp usually is meaningful enough
to get some idea of where to look. In this case, "expecting a single
value" means that, at some point, C++ was expecting a single value
from an R function you provided, but didn't get it. What did it get?
Extent=0 means that no value, that is, NULL. Example:

t <- trajectory() %>%
  timeout(function() NULL)

simmer() %>%
  add_generator("dummy", t, at(0)) %>%
  run()
#>  Error in run_(private$sim_obj, until) :
#>   Expecting a single value: [extent=0].

So review your trajectories and try to find out which function is
returning a NULL value for a longer run time.

> helpful.

> Thanks in advance,

Hi.

I've been trying to create a user-defined function to run a simulation and then save the get_mon data to disk. On Sunday, April 22, 2018 at 1:32:07 PM UTC+1, Iñaki Úcar wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I've just merged this new feature into the master branch. Monitoring
> has always been performed in-memory, which is convenient and fast, but
> may lead to memory issues for very long simulations. Now, it is
> possible to offload this to disk:
>
> library(simmer)
> to_csv <- monitor_csv()
> env <- simmer(mon=to_csv)
> env
> #> simmer environment: anonymous | now: 0 | next:
> #> { Monitor: to disk (delimited files) }
> #>  { arrivals: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_arrivals.csv }
> #>  { releases: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_releases.csv }
> #>  { attributes: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_attributes.csv }
> #>  { resources: /tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_resources.csv }
>
> As you can see, data tables are saved into the R tempdir by default,
> although it is possible to specify any valid location (see
> "?monitor_csv()"). Functions get_mon_arrivals() and the like will work
> as usual to load these files into data frames. However, if you want to
> process the data in a separate workflow, then you can obtain the file
> names from the monitor object:
>
> to_csv$handlers
> #>                                    arrivals
> #>  "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_arrivals.csv"
> #>                                    releases
> #>   "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_releases.csv"
> #>                                  attributes
> #> "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_attributes.csv"
> #>                                   resources
> #> "/tmp/RtmpEew5ES/file29758c1c246_resources.csv"
>
> I'd appreciate if you can test this feature and provide your feedback
> before the next release, which will be in two weeks.
>
> Regards,
> Iñaki
